about: The real case (2026-11-19): chapter 1 of the step 'Circuits from first principles' of the Roadmap 'Build your own gadgets' as it was published — its six sections and three of its exercises, verbatim. Section 1 is about charge, yet it converts mAh to coulombs, and its exercises ask about amperes, volts and joules; current and the ampere are introduced only in section 2, voltage in section 4, energy in chapter 2. tests/gradual.js gives it the concept list an honest author would write for the text as it is and expects Q0 to catch it.

chapter.title: Charge, voltage and current as physical quantities

sections.title: Charge and the coulomb
sections.hook: Every circuit is charge being pushed around: get its units straight first.

blocks.text: Electric charge comes in two kinds, positive and negative. Like charges repel, unlike charges attract.
The unit is the **coulomb (C)**. One electron carries −e with e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C, so 1 C is about 6.24×10¹⁸ electrons.

blocks.title: Charge is quantised and conserved
blocks.text: Charge never appears or vanishes in a circuit. Everything you will do with Kirchhoff's current law is this one sentence.
Battery makers do not quote coulombs but **ampere-hours**: 1 Ah = 1 A × 3600 s = 3600 C, so 1 mAh = 3.6 C.

blocks.label: Think first: how many coulombs are stored in a 2000 mAh cell?
blocks.text: 2000 mAh = 2 Ah = 2 × 3600 C = 7200 C. Note that this is charge, not energy: energy needs the voltage too (chapter 2).

sections.title: Current and its direction
sections.hook: Half of all sign mistakes come from not knowing what the arrow means.

blocks.text: Current is the rate at which charge crosses a surface: $I = \frac{dQ}{dt}$. For a constant current, $Q = I\,t$.
Inversely, the charge that passed between two instants is the area under the current: $Q = \int I\,dt$. This is the idea behind a battery's 'coulomb counter'.
**Conventional current** points the way positive charge would move. In a metal the movers are electrons, so the real motion is opposite to the arrow.

blocks.caption: Conventional current (top) and electron motion (bottom) in the same loop

blocks.text: The sketch shows one loop: the top wire leaves the battery's + terminal and the arrow ► is conventional current. In the same loop the electrons really drift the other way, ◄.
Both descriptions are the same physics. The lesson: pick the conventional arrow and use it everywhere, as every datasheet and every diode symbol does.

head: Conventional current
Electron flow
rows: datasheets, simulators, all equations in this course
exact for metals; in semiconductors holes move the other way

blocks.title: Through versus across
blocks.text: Current flows **through** a part; voltage exists **across** it. 'The voltage through the resistor' is a category error that hides real mistakes.

blocks.label: Think first: in salt water, Na⁺ ions move right and Cl⁻ ions move left. Which way is the conventional current?
blocks.text: To the right, for both: positive charge moving right and negative charge moving left both carry positive charge rightward.

sections.title: Drift velocity versus signal speed
sections.hook: Why does a lamp light instantly if electrons crawl at a tenth of a millimetre per second?

blocks.text: In a wire of cross-section $A$ with $n$ free electrons per m³, a current needs $I = n\,q\,v_d\,A$. So the drift speed is $v_d = \frac{I}{nqA}$.
Copper has $n \approx 8.5\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$. For 1 A in 1 mm²: $v_d = 1/(8.5\times10^{28}\cdot1.6\times10^{-19}\cdot10^{-6}) \approx 7.4\times10^{-5}$ m/s, about 0.07 mm/s.

blocks.title: A pipe full of marbles
blocks.text: Push one marble in at one end and one pops out at the other almost at once, although each marble moved a tiny step. The wire is already full of charge carriers everywhere.
The disturbance travels as an electromagnetic wave guided by the wire: about 0.5 to 0.99 of the speed of light, depending on the insulation. On FR-4 board about 15 cm per nanosecond.
Energy is not carried by electrons marching to the lamp. It flows in the fields around the wire, and the electrons are the medium that sets those fields up.
In 50 Hz mains with 1 A rms in 1 mm², electrons only swing about ±0.33 µm: they never leave the wire.

blocks.label: Think first: you halve the wire cross-section but keep 1 A. What happens to the drift speed?
blocks.text: It doubles, because $v_d \propto 1/A$: the same charge per second has to squeeze through less area.

sections.title: Voltage, reference nodes and 'ground'
sections.hook: '5 V' means nothing until you say 5 V relative to what.

blocks.text: Voltage is energy per charge: $V = \frac{dW}{dQ}$, 1 V = 1 J/C. The voltage between A and B is the work needed to move 1 C from B to A.
It is always a **difference between two points**. When someone says 'node A is at 5 V', they silently mean 'relative to the reference node'.

Reference at battery −            Reference moved to node A

  +9 V ─┬─ R1 ─ A ─ R2 ─┬─ 0 V       +4.5 V ─┬─ R1 ─ A(0 V) ─ R2 ─┬─ −4.5 V
   9 V  battery 9 V     │               battery 9 V                      │
        └───────────────┘                    └──────────────────────────┘
  V(A) = 4.5 V ;  V(R1) = 4.5 V       V(A) = 0 ;  V(R1) = 4.5 V (unchanged)
blocks.caption: The same loop, two reference choices

blocks.text: A 9 V battery feeds two equal resistors in series. On the left the reference is the battery's minus: node A reads 4.5 V. On the right we declare A to be 0 V: the battery's plus is now +4.5 V and its minus −4.5 V.
Look at the last line: every node voltage changed, but the voltage across R1 is still 4.5 V, and so are currents and powers. Moving the reference never changes the physics.

blocks.title: Three different 'grounds'
blocks.text: **Earth** is a safety connection to the soil (the PE wire). **Chassis** is the metal case. **Circuit reference (0 V)** is the node you chose. One drawn symbol can mean any of them, and a battery gadget has no earth connection at all.

blocks.title: Why a bird is safe on a power line
blocks.text: Both feet touch the same wire, so the voltage between them is almost zero and almost no current crosses the bird. The danger is a path between two different potentials.

blocks.label: Think first: you move the reference to a different node. Does a resistor's current change?
blocks.text: No. Current depends on the voltage across the resistor, a difference, and differences do not depend on where zero is placed.

sections.title: The passive sign convention
sections.hook: Fix the signs once, and a negative answer becomes information instead of panic.

blocks.text: For any two-terminal part, you choose a voltage polarity (+ and −) and a current arrow. These are references, not claims about reality.
If the current arrow **enters the + terminal**, you have the **passive sign convention**. Then $p = v\cdot i$ is the power **absorbed** by the part.

i                   i
   ──────►──┐             ┌──►──────
        +   │             │   +
          [ part ]  v     [ part ]  v
        −   │             │   −
   ──────────┘             └──────────
  passive: i enters +     active: i leaves +
  p = v·i absorbed        p = v·i delivered
blocks.caption: Passive versus active reference

blocks.text: Left: the arrow flows into the plus terminal, so $v\cdot i > 0$ means the part is absorbing energy (a resistor always does). Right: the arrow leaves plus, so the same product is power delivered, which is how a source is often drawn.
Ohm's law $v = iR$ is only valid in the passive convention. With the opposite arrow it becomes $v = -iR$, a favourite source of lost minus signs.

Meaning

blocks.title: Ask yourself before writing any equation
questions: Does every part have a voltage polarity and a current arrow drawn?
Does the arrow enter the + terminal of each load (passive)?
Which sign does Ohm's law need for THIS pair of references?

blocks.label: Think first: a 3.7 V cell shows v = +3.7 V and i = −0.5 A in the passive convention. Is it charging or discharging?
blocks.text: p = 3.7 × (−0.5) = −1.85 W: it delivers power, so it is discharging. The real current leaves the + terminal.

sections.title: Water analogy, DC and AC
sections.hook: A good analogy is a loan: useful, but you must know when to give it back.

head: Electric
Water
Where the analogy breaks
rows: pressure has no sign convention or reference choice
charge is never 'used up': what leaves returns
pipe friction is nonlinear, a metal resistor is linear
a pump cannot reverse polarity and leak: a battery can be charged and shorted

blocks.text: Use it for first intuition: more resistance, less flow for the same pressure. Drop it when you need exact behaviour, such as fields, induced voltages or open circuits.
**DC** keeps its sign. **AC** alternates sign, like mains: 230 V **RMS**, 50 Hz in Europe, so the peak is $230\sqrt2 \approx 325$ V.
**Pulsating DC** (rectified mains, PWM) never changes sign but is not constant. It is a DC part plus an AC part, and a meter reading depends on which part it sees.

blocks.label: Think first: what is the peak voltage of 230 V RMS mains?
blocks.text: $230\sqrt2 \approx 325$ V, and peak-to-peak is about 650 V. Insulation must withstand the peak, not the RMS figure.

exercises.q: A constant current of 1 A moves exactly 1 coulomb past a point every second.
exercises.explain: That is the definition of the ampere as one coulomb per second. Students sometimes remember it as 'amps are energy', which is wrong: energy needs voltage as well.

exercises.q: A cell is labelled 2000 mAh. How many coulombs of charge does that label correspond to?
exercises.explain: 2000 mAh = 2 Ah, and 1 Ah = 3600 A·s. So the charge is 2 × 3600 = 7200 C; forgetting the 3600 s per hour is the classic slip.

exercises.q: Match each unit to the quantity it measures.
exercises.explain: The four units chain together: A = C/s and V = J/C. Remembering the chain means you can rebuild any of them from the others.

The direction positive charge would move; electrons in a metal move the other way.
The slow average speed of the charge carriers in a wire.
Energy per charge between two points, 1 V = 1 J/C.
The node chosen as 0 V; every other node voltage is measured from it.
